content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles continual learning with transformers, and has a specific focus on prototype based methods. More specifically, the authors argue that prototypes (i.e. mean of embeddings of each class), that are widely used to perform inference in continual learning setting by nearest neighbor, suffer two issues in incremental learning settings: i) semantic drift, i.e. the parameters change and examples of the class get far from the prototype and ii) interference, i.e. new task examples fall close to the past class prototypes. To solve both in the context of vision transformers, the authors introduce several techniques. First, a group of task specific learnable tokens, called prompts, that will be used in a custom inference procedure. Then, a constrastive loss function to pull examples of the same class closer together and push other class further away. Finally, the authors employ multi-centroid prototypes that can better characterize the embeddings distribution. Experiments are conducted on Cifar100, SplitImagenet and 5 Datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
- +The proposed model seems technically novel to me, and the utilization of prompt task specific tokens in the context of continual learning is interesting and appealing. The model clearly outperforms DualPrompt, the only previous model using the same technique.
- +The experimental results are extremely encouraging, with the model being able to outperform rehearsal based methods in many settings.
- -The biggest weakness of the paper is its clarity. To the best of my effort, I couldn't exactly understand neither:
  - Eq. 6: the equation is complicated. First, it features multiple assignments that might be split into two different equations. Then, I struggle understanding how $P(i)$ is defined. What is $i$? and why does the class $k$ appear to the right but not to the left? How does $P(i)$ relate to the class $k$? 
  - The inference procedure: the text claims that it restores the model's snapshot. Does that happen exactly, meaning that the class prototypes are exactly the same as the ones computed just after their task? If so, the text does not explain why this is the case. Or are they just an approximation?
- -Another weakness is that the model builds on top of transformers specifically, and cannot directly be applied to other architectures such as CNNs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- C: As mentioned above, I had a hard time understanding the details of the proposed model. I advise the authors to revise the math and the text to make it more clear.
- Q: besides the clarity, the quality of the work is very high, with clear motivations, related work discussion, lots of experiments with proper baselines, good results and clear ablation studies.
- N: seems novel to the best of my judgement. One concern is that it builds on top of DualPrompt, yet it features a new contrastive loss objective that proves beneficial.
- R: as a consequence of the low clarity, reproducibility also lowers a bit. In terms of implementation details and training details, proper discussions can be found in the text and in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this submission as borderline. It features excellent and impressive results, yet it it hard to assess the contributions as the model section is not very clear to me. Overall, I think the strenghts outnumber the weaknesses.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer frDv
content.comment:
We cordially appreciate your comments. Thanks for pointing out the unclarity in Eq. 6. We clarified the subscripts in the paper for Eq.6 and made it more accessible. The code will be released to ease future reproduction.

\
*__Q1: Clarification for Eq.6__* 

__Answer:__ $i$ is the index of a data sample belonging to class $k$ in a given mini-batch of images. $P(i)$ denotes the set of all positive samples w.r.t. the data sample $i$ in the current mini-batch, i.e., a collection of all data samples with label $k$ in the current mini-batch. In general, we are pulling together samples with the same label while pushing away data samples with different classes. Along the way of this contrastive force, we also pull samples to their corresponding key prototypes (positive anchors) while pushing away samples from value prototypes (negative anchors) from other classes. 

\
\
*__Q2: “The inference procedure: the text claims that it restores the model's snapshot. Does that happen exactly, meaning that the class prototypes are exactly the same as the ones computed just after their task? If so, the text does not explain why this is the case. Or are they just an approximation?”__*

__Answer:__ We restore snapshots of the model exactly (not an approximation). During inference, our method restores/reemerges the snapshots of the model by combining the frozen embedding function with retrieved task-specific prompt groups. Specifically, given a snapshot of the model after learning a task, we decompose the model into a frozen global model and a task-specific learnable prompt group. During inference, we can restore this exact snapshot by combining them. 

\
\
*__Q3: “Another weakness is that the model builds on top of transformers specifically, and cannot directly be applied to other architectures such as CNNs. "__*
					
__Answer:__ We agree that it is non-trivial to directly migrate our method to other architectures since prompt-tuning is a transformer-specific technique. Thanks for pointing out this valuable future direction regarding generalizing our framework to broader architectures.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer YaMZ
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate your comments and affirmation of our work. Thanks for bringing up these two valuable questions which provide us a chance to further elaborate on these underlying concepts. We hope that the following responses can address your questions.

\
*__Q1: “It is not clear to me what is the training-free baseline. Did you propose it or is it an existing approach? Why is it a good baseline?”__*

__Answer:__ We proposed this simple baseline. Concretely, we leverage a fixed embedding function (a frozen pre-trained ViT in our context) to generate a prototype for each class as well as extract embeddings of data samples. Then the NCM classifier is used to perform classification. Since no trainable parameter exists, it is training-free. It is a good and also important baseline because it explicitly isolates the contribution of the fixed embedding function which serves as one of the critical components in our framework. We can clearly and fairly see the improvements of other proposed modules upon this baseline model and ablate how different pre-training methods affect the final performances (see Table 4).

\
\
*__Q2: “It is not clear to me when/why the method restores the model's snapshot”__*
					
__Answer:__ During inference, our method restores/reemerges the snapshots of the model by combining the frozen embedding function with retrieved task-specific prompt groups. Specifically, given a snapshot of the model after learning a task, we decompose the model into a frozen global model and a task-specific learnable prompt group. During inference, we can restore this exact snapshot by combining them.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Originality and Quality 
#### Strengths
* Prompt tuning has recently been gaining attention for continual learning; therefore, the formulation of task-specific prompts might interest the CL community.
* The proposed contrastive prototypical loss is novel that encourages the alignment between same class embeddings, prototypes and dissimilarity between embeddings, prototypes from different classes. Further, the proposed multi-centroid prototype strategy is interesting.

#### Weaknesses
* I am concerned about the scalability and practicality of the proposed method. The requirement of a group of fictitious embeddings for each class distribution seems like a significant overhead. Furthermore, the proposed method won’t be scalable with many classes and the absence of labels.
* The paper is also limited to transformers-based architectures. While they have been gaining attention for CL, they often underperform in small-dataset regimes. 
* The gains provided by CPP loss in comparison to the SupCon loss are relatively marginal. Was a similar behavior observed for other datasets?
* For split ImageNet, the comparison was conducted against only the prototype-related methods.

### Clarity
Overall, I found the paper well-written and easy to follow, and I have no significant concerns.

### Reproducibility
 The code is not provided with the submission. Since the paper is empirical, it is necessary to provide the code to aid the reproducibility of future works.

content.title: Reply to Reviewer gkaF
content.comment:
Dear reviewer, we greatly appreciate your comments and thank you for supporting our work. The code will be made publicly available. We hope that the following responses can clarify your concerns. 

\
*__Q1: “The requirement of a group of fictitious embeddings for each class distribution seems like a significant overhead. Furthermore, the proposed method won’t be scalable with many classes and the absence of labels.”__*

__Answer:__ We argue that the overhead introduced by fictitious embeddings (multi-centroid prototypes) is not significant and our model is scalable with a considerable amount of classes. For example, since prototypes are highly concentrated information, saving 5-centroids prototypes for the entire split CIFAR-100 dataset only costs 0.77 MB of memory, which is equivalent to the memory cost of 5 ImageNet images (with size 224 x 224 x 3). Therefore, we believe it is fair to say that our method is benign to scalability issues in terms of memory usage given a modern computational architecture. We kindly refer to *Appendix F* for a detailed calculation and discussion about scalability from where we can see that prototypes also have advantages in reducing computational costs and protecting privacy. The absence of labels (we assume you mean few-shot or unsupervised continual learning) is indeed beyond the scope of the current method, which should be a promising future direction. 

\
\
*__Q2: “The paper is also limited to transformers-based architectures. While they have been gaining attention for CL, they often underperform in small-dataset regimes. "__*

Answer: We agree with your concern about the limitation of transformer-based architectures since it is not clear how to directly migrate prompt-tuning techniques to other architectures (e.g., CNNs) in the current paper. Thanks for pointing out this valuable future direction toward generalizing our framework to broader architectures.

\
\
*__Q3: “The gains provided by CPP loss in comparison to the SupCon loss are relatively marginal. Was a similar behavior observed for other datasets?”__*
				
__Answer:__ In our humble opinion, the benefit of CPP loss is consistent and clear. Please see the following table for comparisons between CPP loss and SupCon on all datasets. We want to kindly emphasize that, given our framework design, the average accuracy for each dataset is around 90% with a largely reduced gap between offline joint-learning methods and ours. From the aspect of gaps between upper-bound, split CIFAR-100 for instance, CPP loss reduces the gap between joint learning from 2.25% to 1.42% which is a 36.89% relative improvement. Therefore, due to the boundary decreasing effect, we believe it is fair to say that around 0.8% absolute improvement is a clear and non-trivial improvement. 

||Avg acc (%) | | |
|:------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:| 
| | split CIFAR-100  |  5-datasets | split ImageNet-sub |
| Joint learning|  90.85  |   93.93    |  94.22 |
| SupCon         |  88.6   |  92.5  |  93.36 |
| CPP loss  |  89.43|  93.36 |  93.9 |

\
\
*__Q4: “For split ImageNet, the comparison was conducted against only the prototype-related methods.”__*

__Answer:__ In this rebuttal, we add a new baseline by reproducing DualPrompt with MAE pre-training on the split ImageNet-subset. DualPrompt is, to our best knowledge, the state-of-the-art method for rehearsal-free continual learning which also uses a pre-trained transformer architecture and the prompt-tuning technique. The results are shown in the following Table. We can see that our method outperforms DualPrompt by a clear margin. We believe this result can further justify the advantage of our framework. We refer to *Appendix G* for reproduction details.

|Method|  Avg acc(%)  | Forgetting(%)| 
|:---------|:-----------:|:-----------:|
| DualPrompt (MAE)  | 92.5  | 2.0  |
| CPP (ours) |   93.9    |  1.89 |

content.title: Reply to Reviewer n83G
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our work. Your summary and insightful comments indeed capture the essence of this work. We hope the following responses can address your concerns. The code will also be made publicly available.

\
*__Q1: “Is it necessary to use key prototypes? Since they suffer from semantic drifts, why not use value prototype in the coarse retrieval stage?”__*

__Answer:__ Yes, it is necessary to use key prototypes. Because the query of a data sample and its corresponding key prototype is generated from the same distribution while value prototypes are not. Using value prototypes for the coarse retrieval stage will hamper the performance of the query function and thus degenerate the final performance. As shown in the following table, we observe a clear performance drop without using key prototypes. Please also refer to Fig.7 (d) and Fig.8 (d) in Appendix K, where we can see a clear visual shift between the embeddings of data samples (without adding prompts) and value prototypes under the t-SNE plot.

| Name | Avg acc (%) | Forgetting (%)|
| :---        |    :----:   |   :---: |
| w/o key prototype | 87.15 | 4.31 |
| w/ key prototype   | 89.43 | 3.61 |

\
\
*__Q2: “In Table 2, DualPrompt and CPP use pre-trained backbone for incremental tasks. However, Dytox and DER, in the original papers, use a train-from-scratch strategy. This comparison seems unfair to me. Or, did you reimplement them? Please specify it in the paper.”__*

__Answer:__ We take the results of DER and Dytox from DualPrompt and Dytox’s original paper, respectively. Following your suggestion, we updated how the results are collected and whether they use pre-trained weights in Table 2. In our humble opinion, we believe it is a fair comparison. In Table 2, we compare our method against multiple architecture-based methods whose algorithms are correlated to the design or the selection of their architectures as well as their weights. So it is hard to make a direct comparison under transformer structures without a loss of fairness. Some customized architectures (e.g., in Dytox) simply do not have available pre-trained weights. Instead, we adopt the relative difference metric used in DualPrompt that measures the difference between a method and its own upper-bound under the same configuration. This measurement is expected to offset the influence of other factors if they exist.

\
\
*__Q3: “Does this mean that the model would forward multi-times with different prompt groups? This seems to have a great memory and computation cost. ”__*

__Answer:__ Yes, the model will forward multi-times with different prompt groups, but the costs are affordable. For example, on split CIFAR-100, each data sample is on average associated with 4.4 prompt groups. We kindly note that, even though efficiency is not our main focus, the cost is posed as a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency through query radius in the current design. One can maneuver the actual cost according to their application needs. For future work, it remains a promising direction to further improve efficiency in terms of both algorithm design and engineering implementation.

content.title: Select prompt during inference
content.comment:
Hi author

Thanks for the interesting work! 

I have one question regarding the inference phase. Since this work use deep prompt, all samples per batch need to use the same prompt. However, during testing, each sample may query different prompt because they may from different task. Thus, it is little bit tricky how to select a prompt form a batch. I wonder how this problem is solved in this work.

replying_to: Replying to Select prompt during inference

content.title: Reply to Yuansheng Zhu
content.comment:
Hi Yuansheng,

Thanks for your interest in our work!

During inference, we leverage key prototypes as keys and the class token of the target data sample as query to retrieve a group of candidate prompt groups. Then we combine the target data sample with different retrieved prompt groups to generate a group of fine-grained queries which are then used to do classification based on distances (similarities) between them and value prototypes.
